the-safety-vs-performance-trade-off.core: Concurrent code must be correct when operations interleave unpredictably. Locks make critical sections safe but serialise work and add contention; finer-grained locks, lock-free structures and immutability improve throughput but increase complexity. Start safe, measure, then optimise hot spots.

first_principles.problem: A counter incremented by 8 threads ends at 6.2 million instead of 8 million.

analogy.title: A single-lane bridge
analogy.story: A traffic light keeps it safe but cars wait; a second lane costs construction.
analogy.breaks: Bridges fail loudly; race conditions corrupt data silently.

steps.label: Optimisation
steps.detail: Per-thread local counts, summed at the end: no contention.

code.text:
import threading
lock = threading.Lock()
count = 0
def work():
    global count
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        with lock:
            count += 1

points: Shared mutable state is the danger.

check.q: Why is count += 1 unsafe across threads?
check.a: It reads, adds and writes separately; interleaved threads can overwrite each other's updates.

the-reader-writer-lock.core: A reader-writer lock allows many concurrent readers or one exclusive writer. It boosts throughput for read-heavy data like caches and config, but naive versions can starve writers, so fair implementations block new readers once a writer is waiting.

first_principles.problem: A config map read 10,000 times/sec and updated once a minute is bottlenecked by a mutex.

analogy.title: A museum exhibit
analogy.story: Many visitors can look at once, but when curators rearrange it, the room is closed.
analogy.breaks: Museums schedule closures; writer starvation happens if visitors never stop arriving.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Readers in parallel; waiting writers get priority.

check.q: How can a reader-writer lock starve writers?
check.a: If new readers keep acquiring the shared lock, the reader count never reaches zero for the writer.

the-dining-philosophers-resource-content.core: Five philosophers each need both neighbouring forks to eat. If all pick up their left fork at once, everyone waits forever: deadlock. Deadlock needs four Coffman conditions together (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait), and breaking any one prevents it.

first_principles.problem: A service freezes intermittently when two threads lock accounts A and B in opposite orders.
truths: Holding one lock while waiting for another risks cycles.

analogy.title: Four cars at a four-way stop all edging forward
analogy.story: Each waits for the car to its right, and nobody moves.
analogy.breaks: Drivers eventually wave each other on; threads never give up without timeouts.

check.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

breaking-the-deadlock-resource-ordering.core: The simplest deadlock prevention is a global lock order: always acquire locks in a consistent order (e.g. by account ID or memory address). With no thread ever waiting 'backwards', circular wait can't form. For dining philosophers, everyone picks the lower-numbered fork first.

first_principles.problem: Transfers between accounts deadlock depending on the transfer direction.
truths: Cycles need some thread to acquire in reverse order.
A total order forbids reverse acquisition.
derivation: Encapsulate in a **helper** so callers can't get it wrong.
Use **try-lock with backoff** where ordering is impossible.

analogy.title: Everyone climbs the stairs in the same direction
analogy.story: If people only go up a one-way staircase, they never block each other face to face.
analogy.breaks: Stairs are physical; code paths acquiring locks indirectly can violate the order unnoticed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A→B and B→A both lock the lower ID first: no cycle.

code.text:
def transfer(a, b, amount):
    first, second = (a, b) if a.id < b.id else (b, a)
    with first.lock:
        with second.lock:
            a.balance -= amount
            b.balance += amount

check.q: Why does consistent lock ordering prevent deadlock?
check.a: It removes circular wait: no thread can hold a higher lock while waiting for a lower one.

atomic-operations-and-lock-free-programm.core: CPUs provide atomic instructions (fetch-and-add, compare-and-swap) that update memory indivisibly. Lock-free algorithms loop on CAS (read, compute, CAS; retry if changed), avoiding lock contention and deadlock, but they're hard to get right (ABA problem, memory ordering) and best left to proven libraries.

first_principles.problem: A heavily contended counter spends most time waiting on a mutex.
truths: Hardware can make single-word updates atomic.
CAS succeeds only if the value is unchanged.

analogy.title: Editing a shared doc with 'only save if unchanged since I opened it'
analogy.story: If someone else saved first, reload and retry your edit.
analogy.breaks: Docs show who changed things; ABA means the value can change and change back unnoticed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No locks; threads retry on conflict.

check.a: A value changes from A to B and back to A, so CAS succeeds even though the state changed in between.
